note: Athens has no realm on the base map, so its empire is drawn as occupied areas over the Aegean; circles mark single allied cities. All areas and arrows are approximate reconstructions from campaign maps and Thucydides, and many dates within a year are approximate (ancient sources give seasons, not days).

chapters.title: Plataea and the invasions of Attica
arrows: Spartan invasion of Attica (431 BCE)
Spartan invasion of Attica (430 BCE)
chapters.text: The war began on 4 April 431 BCE when Thebes, Sparta's ally, attacked Plataea, a small city allied to Athens. In early summer the Spartan king Archidamus led the Peloponnesian army into Attica and camped at Acharnae, burning crops within sight of Athens. Pericles kept the Athenians behind their walls and relied on the fleet. When the Spartans returned in 430 BCE and ravaged Attica as far as Laurion, plague broke out in the crowded city.

chapters.title: Pylos and Sphacteria
arrows: Demosthenes sails to Pylos and fortifies it (425 BCE)
Spartans rush back from Attica and land on Sphacteria (425 BCE)
Cleon and Demosthenes storm Sphacteria (425 BCE)
chapters.text: In spring 425 BCE the Athenian general Demosthenes fortified the headland of Pylos on Sparta's own coast. The Spartans hurried back and landed hoplites on the island of Sphacteria, but the Athenian fleet won the battle in the bay and cut them off. After weeks of blockade, Cleon and Demosthenes stormed the island and 292 hoplites, including 120 Spartan citizens, surrendered, a shock that changed the course of the war.

chapters.title: Brasidas in Thrace
arrows: Brasidas marches through Thessaly to Thrace (424 BCE)
Brasidas takes Amphipolis (winter 424 BCE)
Cleon retakes Torone (422 BCE)
Cleon moves on Amphipolis from Eion (422 BCE)
chapters.text: In 424 BCE the Spartan general Brasidas marched the length of Greece to strike at Athens' allies in the north. Acanthus and Stagira came over to him, and that winter he took Amphipolis, Athens' key colony on the Strymon, and then Torone; the historian Thucydides arrived just in time to save the port of Eion. In 422 BCE Cleon retook Torone, but at Amphipolis both he and Brasidas were killed, and the Peace of Nicias followed in spring 421 BCE.

chapters.title: The Sicilian expedition
arrows: Athenian armada sails from Corcyra to Sicily (415 BCE)
Athenians land and seize Epipolae (414 BCE)
Gylippus marches from Himera to Syracuse (414 BCE)
Demosthenes brings a second armada (413 BCE)
Athenian retreat from Syracuse to the Assinarus (413 BCE)
chapters.text: In 415 BCE Athens sent a great fleet to Sicily and wintered at Catana. In 414 BCE the Athenians seized the heights of Epipolae and began to wall Syracuse in, until the Spartan general Gylippus arrived and built a counter-wall. A second armada under Demosthenes failed in a night attack, and after a defeat in the Great Harbour the army retreated on 13 September 413 BCE; within a week it was destroyed at the Assinarus river.

chapters.title: Decelea and the loss of Euboea
arrows: Agis marches out to fortify Decelea (413 BCE)
Peloponnesian fleet off Eretria; Euboea revolts (411 BCE)
chapters.text: In spring 413 BCE the Spartan king Agis fortified Decelea, a day's march from Athens, so that Spartan troops could stay in Attica all year; thousands of slaves escaped and the silver mines stopped. Early in 411 BCE Oropus on the Boeotian border was lost. After a Spartan naval victory off Eretria in September 411 BCE, almost all of Euboea, the island that fed Athens, rose in revolt.

chapters.title: Ionia revolts, Persia pays
arrows: Peloponnesian fleet sails to Chios (412 BCE)
Athenian fleet makes Samos its base (412 BCE)
Peloponnesian fleet wins over Rhodes (411 BCE)
chapters.text: After the disaster in Sicily, Athens' allies across the Aegean began to break away. In summer 412 BCE a Peloponnesian fleet reached Chios, which revolted with Erythrae and Clazomenae, and Miletus followed; Persia's governors now paid for Sparta's ships. Rhodes went over early in 411 BCE. Athens kept its fleet at Samos, which stayed loyal, and held Lesbos and Cos.

chapters.title: The war for the Hellespont
arrows: Mindarus slips into the Hellespont (411 BCE)
Alcibiades' fleet traps Mindarus at Cyzicus (410 BCE)
Alcibiades retakes Selymbria and Byzantium (408 BCE)
chapters.text: Athens imported grain from the Black Sea, so the war moved to the narrow straits. In 411 BCE the Spartan admiral Mindarus made Abydos his base, while Byzantium and Chalcedon revolted from Athens. In spring 410 BCE Mindarus took Cyzicus, but Alcibiades trapped him there; Mindarus was killed and his whole fleet lost. By 408 BCE Alcibiades had won back Chalcedon, Selymbria and Byzantium.

chapters.title: Arginusae and Aegospotami
arrows: Athenian relief fleet to the Arginusae islands (406 BCE)
Lysander sails north and storms Lampsacus (405 BCE)
Athenian fleet follows to Aegospotami (405 BCE)
chapters.text: In 406 BCE Athens rescued its fleet trapped at Mytilene by winning a great sea battle at the Arginusae islands. In 405 BCE the Spartan admiral Lysander, paid by the Persian prince Cyrus, stormed Lampsacus on the Hellespont. The Athenian fleet camped on the open beach at Aegospotami opposite, and Lysander caught it ashore and captured almost every ship. Byzantium, Lesbos and nearly all of Athens' allies then went over to Sparta; only Samos held out.

chapters.title: The surrender of Athens
arrows: Lysander sails for Athens, restoring Aegina (405 BCE)
Pausanias's army camps at the Academy outside Athens (405 BCE)
chapters.text: Without a fleet Athens could no longer bring in grain. Lysander blockaded the Piraeus and gave Aegina back to the people the Athenians had expelled, while the Spartan king Pausanias camped at the Academy outside the walls. Starving, Athens surrendered on 25 April 404 BCE: it pulled down the Long Walls, gave up its fleet and empire, and soon fell under the pro-Spartan Thirty.

battles.name: Battle of Pylos and the siege of Sphacteria
battles.casualties: Of 440 Spartan and allied hoplites on Sphacteria, 148 were killed and 292 captured; Athenian losses were light

battles.name: Battle of Amphipolis
battles.casualties: c. 600 Athenians and 7 Spartans killed, including both commanders, Cleon and Brasidas

battles.name: Destruction of the Athenian army at the Assinarus
battles.casualties: Nearly all of the c. 40,000 people who left the Athenian camp were killed or captured; about 7,000 prisoners were held in the quarries

battles.name: Battle of Aegospotami
battles.casualties: About 160 of 170–180 Athenian ships captured and about 3,000 Athenian prisoners executed; Spartan losses minimal
